INTRODUCTION



With the aim of making the democratic process as transparent as possible to the London electorate,
this report includes a great deal of detail on every aspect of the 2018 London Borough council
elections. No other single volume presents the full results and election statistics from the 32 London
boroughs enabling the reader to analyse and compare the results across London in one place.

The report presents data for every candidate in every ward (excluding the City of London which
operates on a different electoral model). Summaries are provided in the form of maps and tables,
and to make comparisons easier, they mostly match those included in the 2014 report. Results of all
council by-elections between the general elections in 2014 and 2018, as well as details of the
elections in the four boroughs that directly elect a mayor, are also presented here. A commentary of
the results, written by Professor Tony Travers of the London School of Economics, has been
included to give readers an overview of the trends seen in these elections.

The borough elections took place on 3 May 2018 with a turnout of 39 per cent, the same as in 2014.
The number of candidates that stood for election fell to 6,554 (from 6,951 in 2014).

The Conservatives won 511 seats, down 101 from 2014. Meanwhile, Labour made a net gain of 63
seats, takings its total to 1,123 – its highest since 1971. The Liberal Democrats won 154 seats,
making a net gain of 38 and turning around its fortunes after losing a net 163 seats between 2006
and 2014.

Further information about what is included and how to use the report can be found in the Technical
Notes section on page xliii.

This is the latest report in a long series of council election reports dating back to 1964, all of which
are currently available on the London Datastore at: http://data.london.gov.uk/elections

Turnout

The turnout of voters across the 32 boroughs as a whole was 38.8 per cent, a similar level to that
seen in 2014 and 2006 but much lower than seen in 2010, when the turnout was given a boost by
being held on the same day as the parliamentary general elections. The highest and lowest figures
are shown below.

Highest borough                                               Richmond upon Thames         51.4%
Lowest borough                                                Barking and Dagenham         29.5%

Turnout at ward level varied from 25.5 to 57.2 per cent.

COMMENTARY
by Professor Tony Travers
London School of Economics & Political Science



The 2018 London borough elections took place against the backdrop of remarkable political
uncertainty at the national level. All the major political parties were experiencing a degree of turmoil,
generated partly by the consequences of the UK’s 2016 vote to leave the European Union and also
as a result of the unexpected 2017 general election. The latter had resulted in a minority
Conservative government having to initiate the complex process of Brexit. Political turbulence also
derived from challenges by a number of MPs to their national party leaderships and from the changed
nature of individual party memberships.

The Conservatives, Labour and the Liberal Democrats all increased their vote share in 2018, as
compared to 2014. This had also been true in the 2017 general election. Labour saw their share rise
a significant 6.7 percentage points from 37.4 to 44.1 per cent, the Conservatives from 26.1 to 29.0
per cent and the Liberal Democrats from 10.2 to 12.7 per cent. However the number of seats won
by each party across the 32 boroughs, 632 wards and 1,833 seats, does not precisely reflect this
change in share of vote. Labour won a net 63 additional seats, up from 1,060 to 1,123. Meanwhile
the Conservatives, who increased their vote share by 2.9 percentage points, lost a net 101 seats,
down from 612 to 511. The Liberal Democrats gained a net 38, up from 116 to 154.

Overall, Labour’s total of 1,123 councillors is their second-highest ever. The highest was 1,221, in
1971. The Conservatives’ 511 was below their previous lowest total, 519 in 1994, at a time when
they had been in power nationally for 15 years. However, there are now 84 fewer seats than in 1994
due to boundary reviews in some boroughs, which makes this comparison potentially misleading.
The Liberal Democrats’ total of 154 seats was up on the 116 won in 2014, but still well below the
numbers won in every single election between 1986 and 2010.

One of the outcomes of the 2017 general election had been a significant increase in the
Conservative-plus-Labour vote share. Across Britain, this two-party share jumped from 67.2 per cent
in 2015 to 82.3 per cent in 2017. The 2018 London elections followed a similar pattern. The
Conservative-plus-Labour vote across London rose to 73.0 per cent in 2018, up from 63.5 per cent
in 2014. The 2018 figure was the highest Con+Lab total since 1990, when it reached 76.1 per cent.
Only time will tell if the re-emergence of two-party voting (and, indeed, a modest revival in Liberal
Democrat fortunes) is a longer-term trend.

The fact that the three major parties all managed to increase their share of the vote in 2018 was
possible because the smaller ones all lost vote share, especially UKIP. 2014 had seen the ‘Other’
parties win 26.3 per cent of the vote, the highest-ever share. But this number fell to 14.3 per cent in
2018. The Greens, with 8.7 per cent of the vote, did best of the smaller parties, though even their
vote share fell from 9.8 per cent in 2014. UKIP, which won 10.0 per cent of the London vote in 2014,
almost entirely collapsed - no doubt as a result of the Brexit result - and managed only 0.8 per cent
in 2018. As in many previous years, residents’ associations and Independents did better in Havering
than in any other borough.

In terms of geographical strength, Labour’s largest vote share was unsurprisingly in east London,
notably in Barking and Dagenham at 75.1 per cent, followed by 68.0 per cent in Newham and 62.1
per cent in Hackney. The Conservatives’ highest vote share was in outer London: in Hillingdon (52.1
LONDON BOROUGH ELECTIONS MAY 2018                                                                  xxiii




per cent), then Bexley (49.9 per cent) followed, in inner London, by Kensington & Chelsea (48.6 per
cent). For the Liberal Democrats, their best vote share was in their traditional south west London
heartlands of Kingston (49.7 per cent), followed by Richmond (45.2 per cent) and Sutton (37.6 per
cent). The Greens won over 10 per cent of the vote in 12 boroughs, with the highest being 18.5 per
cent in Lambeth. UKIP’s best performance was 6.3 per cent in Havering, though this was down from
28.4 per cent in 2014.

Not surprisingly, the number of seats won by smaller parties fell from 63 in 2014 to 45 in 2018. 24 of
these 45 were elected in Havering. The Greens saw 5 councillors elected in Lambeth (up from one
in 2014) out of a total of 11 (up from 4) across London as a whole. UKIP, by contrast, lost all 12 of
the seats won in 2014 – in Bexley, Bromley and Havering, all outer boroughs.

In terms of the number of votes, on average, required to win a seat, the table below shows the seats
won and votes cast for each of the parties or groupings which won seats in 2018. Labour required
fewest votes to win a seat, with residents’ associations also delivering an efficient votes-per-seat
outcome. Of the parties that won seats in 2018, the Greens enjoyed the least proportionate result,
with over 33,000 votes cast for each seat won. These kinds of outcomes are consequence of the
‘first-past-the-post’ voting system, where the two biggest parties and/or geographically-specific ones
tend to have an efficient ratio between votes cast and seats won.


Table 1: Votes per seat won by political parties in the London local elections, 2018

                                             Seats won            Votes       Votes per seat won
        Conservative                               511        1,958,607                   3,833
        Labour                                   1,123        2,994,259                   2,666
        Liberal Democrat                           154          809,483                   5,256
        Green                                       11          372,768                  33,888
        Residents’ Associations                     25           73,929                   2,957
        Independents                                 8           38,082                   4,760
        People’s Alliance of Tower Hamlets           1           19,580                  19,580




Only three of the 32 boroughs changed political control. Labour gained Tower Hamlets from No
Overall Control, though the borough already had a directly-elected Labour Mayor. The Liberal
Democrats won both Kingston and Richmond from the Conservatives. All other councils remained
with the same political control as in 2014. By contrast, in 2014 seven councils changed control.
Barnet was technically under Minority Control at the time of the May 2018 poll, following the
resignation of a single Conservative councillor during the preceding March. But this proved only a
brief interlude, as the Conservatives decisively regained their majority following the election.

Another consequence of the 2018 borough elections was a further move towards a situation where
a number of councils have little or no opposition. In Barking & Dagenham, Newham and now
Lewisham Labour won all the seats. In Islington, Labour won 47 out of 48 seats, in Tower Hamlets
42 out of 45 and in Brent 60 out of 63. Additionally, in Hackney and Lambeth the opposition won
under 10 per cent of the seats held by Labour. For their part, the Conservatives won 50 out of 60
seats in Bromley. Boroughs which remain more marginal between parties (and thus, presumably,
more politically plural) include Barnet, Croydon, Harrow, Hillingdon, Kensington & Chelsea, Merton,
Richmond, Sutton, Wandsworth and Westminster. Havering, as on several earlier occasions, had a
number of parties, residents’ associations and independents winning seats. The number of
LONDON BOROUGH ELECTIONS MAY 2018                                                               xxiv




politically-marginal boroughs appears to be reducing over time. A year earlier, in the 2017 general
election, Labour had won a number of very large majorities in London constituencies.
Turnout in 2018 was 38.8 per cent, virtually unchanged as compared to 2014, but higher than in
1998, 2002 and 2006. In 2010, London borough elections coincided with a general election, pushing
up turnout to 62.0 per cent. The highest turnout in 2018, 51.4 per cent, was in Richmond, followed
by Kingston (47.3 per cent) and Barnet (43.7 per cent). Richmond perennially has a high turnout.
The lowest turnout, 29.5 per cent, was in Barking & Dagenham, with Southwark at 33.6 per cent and
Lambeth at 34.3 per cent. In Kensington & Chelsea, where the Grenfell Tower fire had occurred in
June 2017, turnout increased dramatically from 30.3 per cent in 2014 to 39.7 per cent in 2018.

The vote took place on a Thursday and a number of counts took place overnight, with results
declared from about 2:00am on Friday morning. Others began counting and declared later on Friday.
London’s population is rising and changing and so is its electorate. The number of people voting
across the city was 2,315,166, the second-highest number ever in a local election year (apart from
2010, when a general election was held on the same day). In 1990, a year when there was national
controversy about local taxation, turnout was high and the number voting in the London boroughs
reached 2,389,455.

There were also four mayoral elections: in Hackney, Lewisham, Newham, and Tower Hamlets. All
four elected Labour Mayors. More information on the mayoral elections can be found on page xxxiii.

The 2018 London borough elections were the 15th such contest since the boroughs were created in
the mid-1960s. Four have never changed control. The Conservatives have always won Kensington
& Chelsea and Westminster, while Labour have always held Barking & Dagenham and Newham.

For the first 30 or so years since the first borough elections in 1964, London generally produced
party vote shares which were similar to those for Britain as a whole. Over time, the Conservatives,
Labour and the Liberals (recast as the Liberal Democrats in 1989) could expect to do as well or badly
in the capital as elsewhere. But since the late 1990s, Labour has begun to win larger votes shares
in London than nationally and, latterly, the Conservatives have done less well in London than across
the country.

The table below shows the vote shares in London and across Great Britain in 2018. The figures for
the country as a whole are called the ‘national equivalent vote share’, which take account of the
varying number and pattern of elections in a particular year and adjusts them to be nationally
representative). They are produced by Professors Colin Rallings and Michael Thrasher and are
taken from the House of Commons Library paper Local Elections 2018. Figures are rounded.


Table 2: Party vote shares in London and Great Britain, 2018

                                            Con        Lab         LD      Others
                   National vote %           37         36          14         13
                   London vote %             29         44          13         14



The Conservatives’ vote in the London borough elections was significantly below their national
performance, while Labour’s was well above. This difference has grown particularly since 2014 when
both Labour’s share (above) and the Conservatives’ share (below) was closer to the national one.
Of course, outside London the opposite is true, with the Conservatives doing relatively better and
Labour relatively worse. London is, as in a number of other ways, diverging from national trends.
LONDON BOROUGH ELECTIONS MAY 2018                                                                 xxv




Borough by borough summary

Labour won every seat in Barking and Dagenham (Lab hold) for the third election in succession.
UKIP’s vote fell from 27.9 per cent in 2014 to zero in 2018 (though no candidates were fielded in this
most recent election). Labour’s vote share rose from 51.1 per cent to 75.1 per cent and the
Conservatives from 9.4 per cent to 21.9 per cent. Labour appear to have gained a larger share of
the former UKIP vote than the Conservatives. Indeed, Labour’s vote share in the borough was the
largest since the highest-ever in 1971 (81.7 per cent). There were no British National Party (BNP)
candidates in a borough where the party had won 12 seats in 2006. At 97 per cent, the Labour-plus-
Conservative share of the vote was the highest-ever in the borough, the highest in London in 2018
and reminiscent of British voting in the 1950s. The Liberal Democrats stood no candidates and thus
their vote share, zero, was the lowest for the party in any borough in 2018.

Barnet (Con hold) was considered a key marginal borough during the 2018 elections, with the
Conservatives being only in minority control at the time of the election. It appears that the national
political controversy involving the Labour party and accusations of anti-Semitism became politically-
salient in Barnet, which has the country’s largest proportion of Jewish voters. In fact, Labour’s vote
increased from 36.7 per cent to 38.6 percent. However, the Conservatives’ vote rose from 38.6 per
cent to 45.1 per cent, leading to a gain of six seats compared to 2014. Thus the Conservatives
moved from a majority of one in 2014 to 13 in the 2018 elections, winning a key seat in Hale ward
and all three seats in West Hendon. The Liberal Democrats lost the one seat they took in 2014, in
Childs Hill, meaning that they have no representation on the council for the first time since 1986.

In Bexley (Con hold), where (as a result of ward and boundary changes) the total number of
councillors fell from 63 in 2014 to 45 in 2018, the Conservatives’ vote share increased from 37.6 per
cent to 49.9 per cent, the highest since 1982. Labour’s share rose from 25.3 per cent to 33.7 per
cent. This change represented a swing of votes from Labour to the Conservatives and continued a
longer-term relative shift from the former to the latter. The UKIP vote in 2014 was 23.4 per cent,
falling to 5.7 per cent in 2018. The 2018 UKIP vote share was the second-highest in London.

Labour further consolidated its control of Brent (Lab hold), gaining four more seats from its 2014
position. The party now holds 60 out of 63 seats, with the Conservatives down to 3. Labour won all
three seats from the Conservatives in Brondesbury Park and one from the Liberal Democrats (the
party’s only seat as of 2014) in Mapesbury. Labour’s vote share was 58.7 per cent, the highest ever
in the borough, while the Conservatives won 21.9 per cent, up slightly on 2014, but well below shares
of over 40 per cent won as recently as the 1990s. The borough has moved from a three-way split of
seats between the Liberal Democrats, Labour and the Conservatives with no overall control as
recently as 2006 to the 2018 position where there are virtually no opposition councillors.

Bromley (Con hold) saw both the Conservatives and Labour increase their vote share. Labour’s
went up from 17.6 per cent in 2014 to 24.0 per cent in 2018, while the Conservatives’ share rose
from 39.6 per cent to 45.4 per cent. Overall, there was a small swing from the Conservatives to
Labour, resulting in Labour gaining one seat (in Clock House ward), though the Conservatives
gained two from UKIP in Cray Valley. However, the Conservatives also lost two to Independents
(former Conservative councillors) in Biggin Hill. But the Conservatives remained dominant, holding
50 out of 60 seats. UKIP’s vote share dropped from 20.2 per cent in 2014 to 2.9 per cent in 2018,
contributing most of the gains enjoyed by the major parties.

Labour gained three additional seats in Camden (Lab hold), with the Liberal Democrats gaining two
and the Conservatives losing five. Labour’s gains were from the Conservatives in Swiss Cottage and
from an independent in West Hampstead, while the Liberal Democrats won seats in Belsize.
LONDON BOROUGH ELECTIONS MAY 2018                                                                    xxvi




Labour’s vote share rose 4.5 per cent, with the Liberal Democrats up 2.6 per cent and the
Conservatives down 0.6 per cent. The Greens won 11.6 per cent of the vote, down from 15.2 per
cent in 2014. Labour clearly benefited from the split nature of the opposition vote and won 43 out of
54 seats, their largest total since 1998. It is only just over 12 years ago that this was run by a
Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition.

In Croydon (Lab hold), the Labour-plus-Conservative vote share reached 84.6 per cent in 2018, up
from 69.4 per cent in 2014 and the highest since 1998. The borough has long been a key marginal
between the two parties, with Labour dominant in the north, the Conservative in the south and the
centre being the main battleground, though in 2014 UKIP won 15.4 per cent. In 2018 the latter’s vote
share dropped to a mere 0.8 per cent. Labour won 41 seats and the Conservatives 29, with
respective vote shares of 44.5 per cent and 40.1 per cent, suggesting politics is still highly-
competitive in the borough. The Labour share was up 8.5 per cent and the Conservatives’ up 6.5
per cent, suggesting that ex-UKIP votes were spread relatively evenly between the two parties. The
2018 election was fought on new ward boundaries, so individual ward change comparisons are
impossible.

Ealing (Lab hold), which for many years was seen as a bellwether for changing shifts of political
fortunes at both a London-wide and national level, saw Labour winning 57 out of 69 seats, the party’s
largest-ever majority (45) on the council. This was only just smaller than the Conservatives’ 46
majority (albeit with a smaller overall number of councillors at the time) in 1968. Labour won seats
in Cleveland, Ealing Common and Northfield wards. Labour’s vote share rose from 48.0 per cent in
2014 to 51.3 per cent, while the Conservatives share fell from 24.5 per cent to 23.3 per cent, the
lowest-ever for the party in the borough. The Liberal Democrats share rose from 8.8 per cent in 2014
to 11.1 per cent in 2018, though this latter figure was still well short of those reached, except in 1990,
between 1982 and 2010.

Labour, the Conservatives and the Liberal Democrats all increased their vote share in Enfield in
2018. Labour were up from 41.7 per cent to 48.5 per cent (up 6.8); the Conservatives increased from
26.0 per cent to 31.1 per cent (up 5.1) and the Liberal Democrats from 2.9 per cent to 7.2 per cent
(up 4.3). The losers were UKIP, and to a lesser extent the Greens. UKIP’s vote share dropped from
11.6 per cent in 2014 to 1.2 per cent in 2018, while the Greens dropped from 11.9 per cent to 9.7
per cent. Labour’s vote share was the party’s highest-ever in the borough, while the Conservatives’
was the second-lowest ever (the lowest was in 2014). Labour’s majority of 29 (46 Labour to 17
Conservatives) in 2018 was up from 19 in 2014. Labour gained seats in Chase, Southgate and
Winchmore Hill. The Conservatives won a seat in Bush Hill Park from Labour.

Greenwich (Lab hold) was again won by Labour, meaning the party has now been in control
continuously since 1971. Labour won 42 out of 51 seats, with the Conservatives winning nine,
reducing Labour’s majority by two. Only one seat, in Eltham North, changed hands, going from
Labour to the Conservatives, even though Labour’s overall vote share rose from 42.3 per cent to
52.2 per cent and the Conservatives’ share increased from 18.3 per cent to 22.0 per cent, suggesting
the Conservatives’ vote in 2018 was more efficiently spread than in 2014. Labour’s vote share was
the highest since the 55.5 per cent won in 1998, though well below the 69.0 per cent won in 1971.

In Hackney (Lab hold), the mayoral election was won by Philip Glanville (Labour) who gained 65.9
per cent of the vote, the highest-ever first-preference vote in a Hackney mayoral election. In the
council election, Labour won 52 seats (up 2) and the Conservatives five (up 1), while the Liberal
Democrats lost the three seats they won in 2014. Labour won seats in Cazenove (from the Liberal
Democrats) while the Conservatives won one from Labour in Stamford Hill. Labour’s vote share rose
from 56.9 per cent in 2014 to 62.1 per cent in 2018, while the Conservatives’ share fell from 12.1 per
cent to 11.3 per cent. The Liberal Democrats marginally increased their vote share, from 8.1 per cent
LONDON BOROUGH ELECTIONS MAY 2018                                                               xxvii




in 2014 to 8.7 per cent in 2018. Labour’s vote share in 2018 was the highest since 1974, whilst the
Conservatives’ achieved their lowest-ever share. The Green Party won 16.8 per cent of the vote,
one of the highest shares in London and came within a small margin of taking a seat in Dalston.

Hammersmith and Fulham (Lab hold) was won by Labour from the Conservatives in a very high
profile campaign in 2014 and retained in 2018. Labour won an additional nine seats in 2018 (up from
26 to 35), while the Conservatives lost nine (down from 20 to 11). Labour won seats from the
Conservatives in Addison, Ravenscourt Park, Sands End and Avonmore & Brook Green. The Labour
vote share increased significantly, from 41.9 to 53.4, with the Conservatives seeing a decline from
38.1 per cent in 2014 to 33.7 per cent in 2018. Labour’s vote share was the highest since 1974,
while the Conservatives received their lowest share since 1986. The Liberal Democrats increased
their vote share from 8.6 per cent in 2014 to 11.0 per cent in 2018, but won no seats. In theory the
borough remains a competitive Labour-Conservative, with any potential longer-term change being
tested in 2022.

The election in Haringey (Lab hold) had been preceded by significant media coverage of very public
disagreements between the 2014-18 Labour leadership and party members about a major
development project. Labour won the council, though lost six seats (down from 48 to 42), while the
Liberal Democrats won six (up from 9 to 15). The Liberal Democrats won seats in Alexandra, Crouch
End, Fortis Green and Muswell Hill in the west of the borough, their traditional heartland. Despite
this change in seats won, Labour’s vote share rose from 48.1 per cent in 2014 to 57.0 per cent, while
the Liberal Democrats’ share increased from 19.9 per cent in 2014 to 23.8 per cent in 2018. The
Conservatives, who as recently as 1990-94 were the main opposition party, saw their vote fall from
9.5 per cent to 7.7 per cent – the lowest Conservative share in any borough in 2018. Labour’s vote
share was the highest since the 1971 election.

Harrow (Lab hold) was held by Labour, though it remained a knife-edge marginal – one of the few
now left in London. Labour gained one seat (up from 34 to 35) while the Conservatives gained two
(up from 26 to 28). The Liberal Democrats lost their sole seat (to Labour in Rayners Lane), as did
two Independents. Labour gained a seat in Harrow-on-the-Hill, while the Conservatives took two in
Headstone North from Independents, while in Kenton East, the Conservatives won two seats from
Labour. Labour’s share of the vote rose from 36.0 per cent in 2014 to 43.9 per cent in 2018, while
the Conservatives’ share increased from 36.5 per cent in 2014 to 42.5 per cent in 2018, implying a
fractional swing from the Conservatives to Labour. The Liberal Democrats’ votes share actually
increased, despite their seat loss.

Of all the boroughs, Havering (NOC hold) has the most fragmented voting pattern, with no party
winning as much as a third of the total vote and thus no party close to majority control. It was the
only NOC council in London in 2018. The Conservatives were the biggest group, with 25 seats,
followed by residents’ associations who won 22. UKIP lost all those they won in 2014, losing a seat
to the Conservatives in Emerson Park, while Labour picked up seats from UKIP in Gooshays and
Heaton wards, winning five in total. The Conservatives won one seat from residents’ associations in
Hylands and one in Saint Andrews. In Hornchurch, Independents gained one from UKIP. The
Conservatives won just under a third of the vote (33.2 per cent), up from 23.1 per cent in 2014.
Labour’s vote share rose from 13.7 per cent in 2014 to 18.4 per cent in 2018. Residents’ vote share
increased from 25.9 per cent in 2014 to 28.6 per cent in 2018. Of the Residents’ 22 seats, eight
represented Hornchurch Residents' Association, six were from Upminster & Cranham Residents'
Association, three from Harold Wood Hill Park Residents Association, three from the Rainham and
Wennington Independent Residents Group and two from the South Hornchurch Independent
Residents Group. In addition, there was one representing the Harold Hill Independent Party and one
Independent. UKIP, who won 28.4 per cent of the vote in 2014, managed just 6.3 per cent in 2018.
These shares were the highest for any borough in each year. UKIP’s decline in vote share appears
LONDON BOROUGH ELECTIONS MAY 2018                                                                xxviii




to have benefited the Conservatives more than Labour. The combined Conservative-plus-Labour
vote in 2018, 51.6 per cent, was the third lowest in London.

Hillingdon (Con hold), whose leader in 2018 was the longest-serving in London, saw a Conservative
gain of two seats from Labour in a borough some thought could swing to Labour. The Conservatives
won 44 seats and Labour 21 with no other party winning seats. Two seats were won by the
Conservatives from Labour the Charville ward and one in Uxbridge South, while Labour gained one
from the Conservatives in West Drayton. The UKIP vote in 2014 had been 19.1 per cent, though this
dropped to zero in 2018 because the party put up no candidates. The Conservative vote share
jumped from 36.0 per cent in 2014 to 52.1 per cent in 2018, while Labour’s share rose from 27.7 per
cent in 2014 to 36.7 per cent in 2018, suggesting that the former UKIP vote moved more to the
Conservatives than Labour. The Conservatives’ vote share in 2018 was the highest since the 52.7
per cent achieved in 1982.

In Hounslow (Lab hold), Labour won 51 out of 60 seats, with the Conservatives winning the other
nine. Labour took two seats from the Conservatives in Osterley & Spring Grove, increasing the
party’s majority from 38 in 2014 to 42 in 2018. Labour’s vote share increased from 43.6 per cent in
2014 to 52.7 per cent in 2018, while the Conservatives’ share rose from 25.0 per cent in 2014 to
28.0 per cent in 2018. Labour’s vote share was the highest since 1994 and the Conservatives’
broadly similar to the average since the same year. The Liberal Democrats’ share rose from 7.3 per
cent in 2014 to 9.0 per cent in 2018, while UKIP’s share dropped from 11.0 per cent in 2014 to zero
(no candidates) in 2018.

Islington (Lab hold) elected 47 Labour councillors and one Green, as in 2014. In the borough where
the Leader of the Opposition has his constituency, Labour’s vote share increased from 54.7 per cent
in 2014 to 59.4 per cent in 2018, the highest since 1974. The Liberal Democrats, who controlled the
borough from 2002 to 2010, won just 12.1 per cent of the vote, behind the Greens on 16.1 per cent.
This was the Liberal Democrats’ lowest vote share since 1990, though the Greens’ share fell
compared to 2014 (from 18.8 per cent to 16.1 per cent in 2018). The Conservatives’ share of the
vote dropped from 9.7 per cent in 2014 to 9.5 per cent in 2018. The latter is actually rather higher
than the party’s share in 1998 (6.0 per cent) and 2002 (3.9 per cent), but falls well short of the 20 -
30 per cent figures reached in the late 1970s and early 1980s.

The 2018 election in Kensington and Chelsea (Con hold) took place in the shadow of the Grenfell
Tower fire which had occurred in June 2017, creating a unique political environment with different
issues at play than in other boroughs. In the event, the Conservatives, who had held the council
continuously since the first borough elections in 1964, won easily, taking 36 out of 50 seats. The
Conservatives lost one seat while Labour gained one (in St Helen’s ward), with the Liberal
Democrats holding their single seat. The Conservatives vote share fell from 52.9 per cent in 2014 to
48.6 in 2018, while Labour’s rose from 27.1 per cent to 32.0 per cent, suggesting they gained more
votes in Labour held wards. The Liberal Democrats’ share increased from 10.4 per cent in 2014 to
12.5 per cent. Given the controversy surrounding the Grenfell Tower fire, the relatively static nature
of the election in the Royal Borough could be thought to be remarkable. The Conservative vote share
had been lower in 1994, while Labour’s was higher in 1971 and 1998.

Kingston upon Thames (Lib Dem gain) produced one of the few major shifts in both seats and vote
shares as compared to 2014 across London. The Liberal Democrats increased their seats held from
19 to 39, while the Conservatives fell from 28 to 9 seats. Labour lost the two they had gained in
2014. The Liberal Democrats’ vote share rose from 26.4 per cent in 2014 to 49.7 per cent in 2018,
a remarkable swing, while the Conservatives’ share dropped from 33.9 per cent in 2014 to 29.4 per
cent. Labour were squeezed, with their vote share declining from 15.1 per cent in 2014 to 11.4 per
cent in 2018. The Liberal Democrats won all the seats from the Conservatives in Alexandra,
LONDON BOROUGH ELECTIONS MAY 2018                                                                xxix




Beverley, Canbury and St James wards, and one or two each in Berrylands, Chessington North &
Hook, Coombe Vale, Grove and Tudor wards. Labour lost their seats to the Liberal Democrats in
Norbiton. This was a ‘landslide’ change in a year with few such results.

Meanwhile in Lambeth (Lab hold), Labour remained dominant, winning 57 out of 63 seats, down
two from the 59 the party won in 2014. However, the Greens won four additional seats, taking their
total to five and making them the largest opposition party. The Conservatives won just one,
compared to three in 2014. Labour took two seats from the Conservatives in Clapham Common,
while the Greens took two from Labour in St Leonards, and one each from Labour in Gipsy Hill and
Herne Hill. Labour’s vote share increased from 50.7 per cent in 2014 to 52.7 per cent in 2018, while
the Greens’ share rose from 14.9 per cent to 18.5 per cent, giving them (as in 2014, though by a
larger margin) the second largest vote share on the council. 18.5 per cent was also the Greens’
highest share in any borough in 2018. The only time Labour has had a higher vote share in the
borough was in 1971, while the Conservatives’ 12.5 per cent was their lowest-ever. The Liberal
Democrats’ vote share, at 11.8 per cent, was fractionally lower in 2018 than in 2014.

A new mayor, Damien Egan (Labour), was elected in Lewisham (Lab hold) following the decision of
his long serving predecessor not to stand again. He won 54.3 per cent of the vote (the highest-ever
share in a Lewisham mayoral election) and was thus elected on ‘first preference’ votes alone. On
the council, Labour won all 54 seats, taking one from the Greens. Thus, the borough joined two other
Labour authorities in London with councillors from only one party. Labour’s vote share rose from
43.1 per cent in 2014 to 53.3 per cent in 2018, though this latter figure is lower than in 1964, 1971,
1974, 1990, 1994 and 1998. But in most of those earlier years, the opposition vote was more
concentrated, particularly (in the 1960s, 1970s and 1980s) when the Conservatives were stronger,
though more recently when the Liberal Democrats had much increased their vote share. In 2014,
there was a substantial vote for the ‘People Before Profit’ party which did not stand candidates in
2018.

In Merton (Lab hold), Labour and the Conservatives lost seats, with the Liberal Democrats winning
five more than in 2014. In both Abbey and Cannon Hill wards, Labour lost a seat to the
Conservatives, while in Dundonald, Trinity and West Barnes the Liberal Democrats picked up seats
from the Conservatives. Residents’ associations held their three seats in Merton Park. The Labour
vote share increased from 43.4 per cent in 2014 to 44.6 per cent in 2018, while the Conservatives’
share rose from 27.6 per cent to 29.9 per cent. The Liberal Democrats’ vote share increased from
9.6 per cent in 2014 to 13.9 per cent in 2018. The Greens’ share of the vote also rose. It appears
that almost all of the 2014 UKIP vote was scattered between the other parties as well as some votes
moving from one of the larger parties to the others. Labour retained overall control with 34 seats and
a majority of 8 over other parties.

Newham (Lab hold) elected a new mayor, Rokhsana Fiaz (Labour), who received 73.4 per cent of
the vote which was the highest-ever first-preference vote share in any London mayoral election since
the original borough mayoral elections in 2002. In the council election, Newham returned 60 Labour
councillors for the third election in a row and the fifth time since 1986. Indeed, only 73 non-Labour
councillors (40 of them before 1971) have ever been elected in the borough, as compared to 827
Labour ones. Labour’s vote share was 68.0 per cent, the highest ever in Newham. The
Conservatives’ vote share was 13.5 per cent, down from 22.2 per cent in 2014, though well above
lower figures in the 1970s. Stratford and New Town was the most contested ward, with Liberal
Democrat and Green candidates polling 1,195 and 1,017 votes respectively, though even here the
lowest Labour vote among the three candidates elected was 2,825.
LONDON BOROUGH ELECTIONS MAY 2018                                                                 xxx




In Redbridge (Lab hold), a borough that used to be a marginal borough saw Labour make substantial
gains, increasing the number of seats held from 35 in 2014 to 51 (+16) in 2018. The Conservatives
lost 13 (down from 25 to 12) and Liberal Democrats three (from three to none). Labour’s vote share
increased from 41.9 per cent to 55.9 per cent. The Conservatives’ share rose from 30.5 per cent in
2014 to 34.2 per cent in 2018. There was thus a 5.1 per cent ‘swing’ of votes from the Conservatives
to Labour which proved sufficient to produce a significant shift of seats from one party to the other.
This kind of result shows how the first-past-the-post voting system begins to squeeze even the
second-biggest party when the party with the largest vote rises much above 50 per cent. The Liberal
Democrats were also squeezed, losing all three of the seats won in 2014 and over half of their 2014
vote share. UKIP won 6.6 per cent of the vote in 2014 but stood no candidates in 2018. Because of
boundary changes, ward-by-ward comparisons are difficult.

As compared to 2014, Richmond (Lib Dem gain) saw an almost complete reversal of fortunes
between the Liberal Democrats and the Conservatives. In 2014, the Conservatives won 39 seats
and the Liberal Democrats 15, whereas in 2018, the Liberal Democrats won 39 seats and the
Conservatives 11, with the Greens picking the other four seats. This pattern of big swings between
the Conservatives and Liberal Democrats in the borough is not new. Similar shifts between one party
and the other occurred in 1986, 2002 and 2006. The Liberal Democrats won seats in East Sheen,
Ham, Petersham & Richmond Riverside, Hampton, Hampton North, Hampton Wick, Heathfield, Kew,
Mortlake & Barnes, North Richmond, South Richmond, South Twickenham, Twickenham Riverside,
West Twickenham and Whitton. In a number of wards, there was a straight switch from the
Conservatives to the Liberal Democrats. The Liberal Democrats’ vote share rose to 45.2 per cent,
up from 28.0 per cent in 2014, whereas the Conservatives’ share dropped from 39.6 per cent in 2014
to 32.2 per cent in 2018. The Greens’ gain of four seats was produced, oddly, by a decline in vote
share from 13.2 per cent in 2014 to 11.6 per cent in 2018. As is sometimes the case in British
elections, a move of votes between two parties can produce accidental benefits for a third. Labour’s
vote share, 8.9 per cent, was their lowest in any borough in 2018, probably squeezed by tactical
voting.

Southwark (Lab hold) was won by Labour, though both they and their main opponents, the Liberal
Democrats, gained vote share and won one additional seat each. For the first time since 1964, the
Conservatives won no seats. Labour’s vote share rose from 44.9 per cent to 52.9 per cent, while the
Liberal Democrats’ share increased from 18.8 per cent in 2014 to 21.5 per cent in 2018, implying a
2.6 per cent ‘swing’ from the Liberal Democrats to Labour. Labour’s share was the highest since
1978, while the Liberal Democrats’ proportion remained below that won in each year from 1982 to
2010. The Conservatives’ vote share, at 10.4 per cent was the lowest-ever for the party in the
borough and contrasts starkly with the 51.6 per cent won in the party’s best-ever year in London
borough elections, 1968, or even with the 28.5 per cent won in 1982. The Greens polled 12.1 per
cent, slightly down on 2014. Because of boundary changes, ward-level gains and losses are not
possible.

In 2014, Sutton (Lib Dem hold) was the only borough won by the Liberal Democrats and it was
retained, albeit with a reduced majority, in 2018, despite it being one of five boroughs in London
which voted for Brexit. The party has now run the borough with a majority continuously since 1990
and was in control of a minority administration from 1986 to 1990. The Liberal Democrats won 33
seats in 2018, down from 45 in 2014, while the Conservatives won 18, up from nine in 2014.
Independents, opposing an incinerator, won three seats in Beddington North from the Liberal
Democrats. The Conservatives gained one seat each in Cheam and Worcester Park and three in
both Nonsuch and Stonecot wards. The Liberal Democrats won a seat from the Conservatives in
Beddington South. The Liberal Democrat majority was cut from 36 to 12. The Liberal Democrats’
vote share increased slightly, from 35.7 per cent in 2014 to 37.6 per cent in 2018, though the
Conservatives’ share rose from 24.7 per cent to 35.2 per cent, implying a swing of over four per cent
LONDON BOROUGH ELECTIONS MAY 2018                                                                 xxxi




from the Liberal Democrats to the Conservatives. Labour’s vote share rose from 12.1 per cent in
2014 to 17.2 per cent in 2018. A UKIP vote of 19.8 per cent in 2014 was reduced to 2.3 per cent in
2018, perhaps suggesting that both the Conservatives and Labour benefited from its decline.

Tower Hamlets (Lab gain) re-elected John Biggs (Labour) as mayor. Biggs had been elected in a
by-election in 2015 following the disqualification of the previous mayor. His vote share in the first
round of voting increased from 40.0 per cent in the 2015 by-election to 48.4 per cent in 2018. He
then won comfortably on second preference votes. In the council election, Labour won Tower
Hamlets from ‘no overall control’, taking 42 seats (the largest total for Labour since 1994) compared
to the 22 won in 2014. Tower Hamlets First, a group linked to the previous mayor but which was
dissolved in 2015, lost all 18 of the seats won in 2014, while the Conservatives lost three of the five
won that year. Labour therefore won 42 out of 45 seats, leaving only three opposition councillors in
total. Labour’s gains from Tower Hamlets First came in Bethnal Green, Bromley North, Canary
Wharf, Lansbury, Mile End, Poplar, St Dunstan’s St Peter’s, Shadwell, Spitalfields & Banglatown,
Stepney Green and Whitechapel. Labour won from the Conservatives in Blackwall & Cubitt Town,
Limehouse and St Katharine’s & Wapping. In Shadwell, the People’s Alliance of Tower Hamlets, a
successor to Tower Hamlets First, won one seat. Labour’s vote share in 2018 was 43.9 per cent,
up from 33.3 per cent in 2014, while the Conservatives’ share fell from 11.3 per cent in 2014 to 10.2
per cent in 2018. The Liberal Democrats, who controlled the council from 1986 to 1994, won just 8.5
per cent of the vote, though this was up from 6.5 per cent in 2014. After a period of considerable
upheaval, the borough’s political landscape returned to relative normality at the 2018 election.

In Waltham Forest (Lab hold), Labour gained two seats from the Conservatives, both in Hale End
& Highams Green. Labour thus won 46 seats in 2018 and the Conservatives 14. The borough has a
strongly Conservative north in Chingford, with Labour winning in the centre and south in
Walthamstow and Leyton, although historically the Liberal Democrats were strong in the centre.
Labour’s share of the vote rose from 43.7 per cent in 2014 to 51.3 per cent, the highest since 1971,
while the Conservatives’ share also rose, from 17.7 per cent to 21.2 per cent. There was thus a two
per cent swing from the Conservatives to Labour. The Liberal Democrats’ share dropped from 12.0
per cent in 2014 to 10.0 per cent in 2018, the party’s worst share since 1978. The Greens’ share
rose from 11.7 per cent in 2014 to 13.3 per cent in 2018, the highest-ever share for the party in the
borough.

Wandsworth (Con hold) was a key political battleground in 2014, as so often in the past. In the 2017
general election, voting in the three Wandsworth constituencies (added together) had produced a
significant majority for Labour. However, a willingness of electors to vote differently locally than
nationally, added to the vagaries of the distribution of voters from ward to ward, meant that the
Conservatives retained control of the council in 2018, albeit with a fractionally lower vote share than
Labour. The Conservatives’ share, at 38.4 per cent was the lowest since 1974, while Labour’s was
their highest at 38.7 per cent since 1994. 2018 was the first year since 1986 when Labour won a
larger vote share than the Conservatives. The Conservatives won 33 seats in 2018 (down eight) and
Labour 26 (up seven), with a single independent winning in West Hill. Labour gained seats from the
Conservatives in Bedford, Earlsfield, Queenstown and West Hill. The Greens’ vote share fell back
in 2018, down to 8.6 per cent in 2018 from 13.0 per cent in 2014. The Liberal Democrats fractionally
increased their share to 7.7 per cent.

The City of Westminster (Con hold), totemic for many reasons and over many years, was the
location of a huge Conservative vs Labour campaign in 2018. The Parliamentary election in 2017
had seen Labour winning the overall vote share in the City’s two seats. In the event, the
Conservatives won a comfortable majority, albeit losing four seats to Labour in Bayswater (1), Maida
Vale (2) and West End (1), though also winning one from Labour in Churchill ward. Thus, the
Conservatives’ total fell from 44 to 41 and Labour’s rose from 16 to 19. The Conservatives’ vote
LONDON BOROUGH ELECTIONS MAY 2018                                                                xxxii




share increased from 40.7 per cent in 2014 to 42.3 per cent in 2018, while Labour’s climbed from
32.8 per cent to 40.3 per cent, suggesting a swing from the Conservatives to Labour of just under
three per cent. The Conservatives have controlled Westminster continuously since the first election
in the mid-1960s. However, the vote difference between the two parties in 2018 was just 2.0 per
cent, the smallest ever. The previous lowest was 3.8 per cent, in 1986. The distribution of votes from
ward to ward still gives the Conservatives an advantage over Labour, but rather less so than in the
past. The Green vote, which rose to 14.3 per cent in 2014, fell back to 5.9 per cent in 2018, though
the Liberal Democrats increased their share from 6.2 per cent in 2014 to 9.0 per cent in 2018.
LONDON BOROUGH ELECTIONS MAY 2018                                                                xxxiii




The 2018 elections and longer-term trends

The 2018 borough elections continued a trend visible since the late-1990s. In many boroughs, there
has been a shift from the Conservatives to Labour which has resulted in them being less marginal
than in the past. Thus, in places like Brent, Camden, Croydon, Ealing, Enfield, Harrow, Lambeth,
Lewisham, Redbridge and Waltham Forest there has been a longer-term trend for Labour to win a
relatively larger share of the vote and the Conservatives to win a smaller one. Some, for example
Croydon, Ealing, Enfield, Harrow and Redbridge are probably still competitive enough for the
Conservatives to win in a year with (for them) a very good election, but not in most others.
Previously, the Conservatives have been better placed to win in an ‘average’ year. Meanwhile, only
Bexley, and possibly Hillingdon, are moving in the opposite direction. That is, over time it appears to
be becoming easier for the Conservatives to win in these boroughs.

Despite the particular challenges of the 2018 election, Kensington & Chelsea is probably now one
of only two truly safe Conservative boroughs, along with Bromley. The Conservative and Labour
vote shares in Wandsworth and Westminster were close enough in 2018 to suggest that in a very
good year for Labour either or possibly both might be vulnerable. Barking & Dagenham, Hackney
and Newham now appear permanently rock-solid for Labour and there are a number of other
boroughs heading this way.

In a number of other boroughs, the relative strength of the Conservatives and Labour seem
reasonably settled in the longer-term. Barnet, Greenwich, Hammersmith & Fulham and Merton see
volatility from election to election, but both the Labour and Conservative votes appear reasonably
consistent over time, even if one of the parties currently dominates.

Where the Liberal Democrats have been successful in past elections there is always a chance that
they will suddenly do better again, for example the landslides achieved in Richmond and Kingston
in 2018. In Tower Hamlets, Islington and Southwark there was no particular evidence of a Liberal
Democrat resurgence in 2018 though the party still has a base of support, especially in the latter two
authorities. Haringey, however, saw a Liberal Democrat revival in 2018, suggesting the party can
still re-appear if one of the major parties is seen as having local difficulties. In Sutton, where the
Liberal Democrats have led the council for over three decades, the Conservatives proved more
competitive in 2018.

Havering is unique. Its politics are unlike those in any other boroughs, with significant numbers of
residents’ and independent councillors. This pattern seems well-established.

Overall, London borough elections have, in recent elections, become somewhat less competitive. It
appears that more boroughs would be likely to remain within one party’s control (particularly Labour)
than in the past. Regardless of political standpoint, the lack of effective opposition is surely
concerning. There are three where all the councillors are from one party, Labour. There are
implications for all the major and smaller parties if this trend were to continue.

LONDON BOROUGH ELECTIONS MAY 2018                                                                                xxxiv




Directly Elected Mayors

Voting in these elections is by the supplementary voting (SV) system. Under this system, voters may
indicate both their first and second choice candidates, and, if no candidate receives an absolute
majority of first-choice votes, all but the two leading candidates are eliminated and the votes of those
eliminated redistributed according to their second-choice votes to determine the winner. In 2018,
only Tower Hamlets required the use of second-choice votes.

The turnouts in each of the four Mayoral elections were broadly the same as in the local elections
and within 4 percentage points of the total turnout rate for London.

John Biggs of Tower Hamlets and Philip Glanville of Hackney were both re-elected as mayors in
their respective boroughs (both were first elected in by-elections between the 2014 and 2018
elections1). In Lewisham and Newham the previous office-holder did not stand, which ensured that
there would be new mayors in those authorities

Philip Glanville was elected in Hackney with 65.9 per cent of the vote. This was slightly below
Glanville’s vote share in the 2016 by-election (68.9 per cent) but above the share of the vote received
by Labour’s winning candidate in 2014 (60.4 per cent).

In Lewisham, Damien Egan was elected with 54.3 per cent of the vote, up 3.5 percentage points
from the Labour vote achieved in 2014.

Newham’s winning candidate Rokhsana Fiaz was elected with 73.4 per cent of the vote. Labour’s
winning candidate in 2014 received 61.2 per cent.

Tower Hamlets’ election required second preference votes. In the first round, Labour candidate John
Biggs achieved 48.4 per cent of the vote compared to second placed People’s Alliance of Tower
Hamlets candidate Rabina Khan’s 16.9 per cent. Biggs was elected after the second round,
achieving 72.2 per cent of the vote to Khan’s 27.3 per cent.

Technical Notes

The London Borough Councils
The London boroughs were constituted under the London Government Act, 1963 and the first
elections to the new councils were held on 7 May 1964. Prior to 1976, councillors were elected at
general elections held every three years but as a result of an order made under the Local
Government Act, 1972, the term of office of members of London borough councils was increased to
four years. Before 1978 each council included aldermen, to a maximum of one sixth of the
councillors, elected by the councillors from among themselves or from persons qualified to be
councillors. Under the Local Government Act, 1972, the office of alderman of a London borough
council ceased to exist after the 1978 elections. The mayor of each borough is elected annually by
each council from among the councillors, with the following exception: under the Local Government
Act, 2000, a council proposing a directly elected mayor must carry out a referendum on its proposals,
the result of which is binding on the local authority.

Following ward boundary changes which became effective on 3 May 2018, the total number of wards
in London increased from 629 to 632 with changes in Bexley, Croydon, Southwark, and Redbridge.
The number of wards per borough varies from 16 in Hammersmith and Fulham, Islington, and
Kingston upon Thames to 28 in Croydon. The number of councillors per borough ranges from 45 in
Tower Hamlets and Bexley to 70 in Croydon. Most London wards return 3 members, however there
are 55 two-seat wards and 4 single-seat wards.


City of London
The Corporation of London is constituted differently to the London boroughs and is, therefore, not
included in the current publication. It consists of common councilmen and aldermen in addition to
the Lord Mayor. The aldermen are elected for life by the ward voters (who include business as well
as resident voters).

Where comparisons have been made between the borough election data and other elections, the
City of London has been excluded from the Cities of London and Westminster constituency and the
North East GLA Assembly constituency.


Tables and calculations
The main results and the share of the votes by party are combined to provide a single section for
each London borough giving all the most important information. This appears between pages 1 and
205.

The general method for calculating share of the votes follows that used in 1994. In calculating vote
share, residents’ associations, independent residents, tenants and residents have been combined
into a single grouping which is given the abbreviation REA in the borough statistics.

All percentage vote figures include a correction to reduce the errors due both to parties or groups
failing to nominate candidates for all seats in a ward, and to the differing numbers of seats in wards
within and between boroughs. The correction chosen is the use of average votes per candidate for
any given party or group. Percentages are based on the sum of average votes for a ward or borough,
which is thus used as an estimate of the total number of valid votes cast in a single seat election.
Percentages do not necessarily add to 100 due to rounding.
LONDON BOROUGH ELECTIONS MAY 2018                                                                  xlv




Candidates’ names
Where known candidates’ principal names are shown as their name as per the electoral roll, and
otherwise are shown as they appear on the nomination papers.


Acknowledgements
Once again we should like to thank the Returning Officers of the London boroughs who supplied the
basic information presented in this volume. Our thanks are also due to the many other members and
officers of the London boroughs who were instrumental in improving the quality of our information.


Maps
The ward map for the 2014 elections shows wards that came into effect on 22 May 2014. The ward
map for the 2018 elections shows boundaries that came into effect on 3 May 2018, which affected
Bexley, Croydon, Southwark, and Redbridge.


General statistics
The General statistics shown on the first page of each borough section are sourced as follows. The
electorates are taken from the data provided for this series of publications by the Returning Officers.
The mid year resident population is from the GLA 2016-based housing-led population projections,
provided by GLA Intelligence Unit. The unemployment rates are from the ONS Model-based
Estimates of Unemployment (April to March). The average council tax data are from the Ministry of
Housing, Communities & Local Government. Additional notes are also provided at the head of
individual sections.


Using the results section
The share of the poll data shown in the results section are based on the average number of votes
per party per ward. For example, if there are three candidates for one party, the total number of votes
for that party would be divided by three, whereas wards with a single candidate would be divided by
one. For the borough and constituency shares, the figures for wards (that is votes divided by
candidates) within those areas are summed.

Gains are shown at the top of the results for each ward and show changes since the last election in
2010. Gains do not include any changes of allegiance or from by-elections.

Candidates marked with an asterisk (*) indicate that the candidate was a sitting councillor in that
ward, i.e. the incumbent. This takes account of changes that occurred from a by-election. Other
points of note: candidates marked in bold were elected, names are shown as surname, then first
name, then initials of any middle names. The names displayed are as provided by the borough
election officers and, in some cases, are nicknames.

Parliamentary constituency comparisons

The following table compares the share of the vote of the major parties, between the 2018 borough
elections and the Westminster parliamentary elections in 2017. This analysis is carried out on a
parliamentary constituency basis.

Most wards fit within the current parliamentary constituency boundaries, however several wards are
split between two or more parliamentary constituencies. In order to make comparisons between
these elections, votes from these wards have been split depending on the proportion of population
aged 18 and over living in each parliamentary constituency, and these are displayed in the table
below.
